Howard Wenger, president of Nextpower, first got interested in solar power during the energy crisis of the 1970s. In his 42-year career in the industry, he has seen an astonishing transformation, as solar has moved from a niche technology for highly specialized applications to a core contributor to meeting electricity demand. In this special episode of Energy Gang from the RE+ conference in Las Vegas, he talks to host Ed Crooks about where the solar industry is now, and where it is going in the future.
Nextpower is a company that provides systems for the solar and storage industries, including trackers, inverters, foundations and electrical balance of system. As Howard says, “everything but the panel for large scale solar power and everything but the battery cell for battery storage.” It is a big player in the industry, providing equipment for 30% of all the power installed in the US last year.
The AI data-center buildout is pushing electricity demand sharply higher, often faster than utilities can deliver grid connections. That creates demand for behind-the-meter power, often as an interim step until a grid connection can be agreed, and solar and storage have a vital role to play. Howard says the debate is often not about solar and storage versus gas, but about how solar and storage and gas can be combined to provide the cleanest possible power as quickly as possible, with the availability and reliability that data center operators demand.
Howard’s argument is that by combining trackers, inverters, foundations, wiring and software into an engineered package, Nextpower can reduce costs, raise output, speed construction and lower project risk. Charged up by rising electricity demand, the business is growing fast. In its capital markets day for investors, held shortly before Howard spoke to Ed, the company raised its target for 2030 revenues by almost 50%, from $5.2 billion to $7.5 billion.
The discussion also goes into the impact of policy uncertainty on solar and storage. With the successes for Democrats in the US midterm elections, speculation has inevitably been on the rise about possible future expansions and extensions of tax credits for renewable energy. But not everyone in the industry is enthusiastic about that prospect.
Howard says Nextpower would be comfortable without clean-energy incentives, if the playing field with fossil fuels were level. However, he adds, the import tariffs and other additional costs placed on solar and storage mean that continued support from tax credits is needed.
What's next is here: Building the future of power infrastructure 
Electricity demand is accelerating, and the infrastructure needed to support it is becoming more complex. 
Nextpower™ (Nasdaq: NXT) is addressing that complexity by bringing together solar power generation, energy storage, power conversion, data intelligence and lifecycle services in one integrated technology platform. 
Building on more than a decade of leadership in utility-scale solar tracking, Nextpower engineers, delivers and supports technologies that help developers, utilities, and asset owners build faster, generate more energy and reduce long-term risk. 
With more than 160 GW of solar technology deployed globally, deep engineering expertise and investment-grade financial strength, Nextpower is helping deliver modern energy infrastructure built to perform for decades.
